Language has three modes: writing, speech, and signs (used by deaf people)
All languages (with the exception of sign language) share a spoken part

## Linguistics:
The science of language or the scientific study of language
A system of communications. It is the phenomenon of vocal and written communication along human beings generally in ordinary usage
Empirically grounded, based on actual language data, observations of language users and their intuitions
*Descriptive not prescriptive*. Aims to describe languages as they are spoken: what they say rather than what they should say

## Branches of linguistics:
*Phonetics*: the way speech sounds are produced, their nature (the physics of sound waves) and how they are perceived. n/k/m/l/p/
*Phonology*: concerned with the ways sounds are patterned (grammar of phonetic patterns). pan, ban, span
*Morphology*: deals with the way the words of a language are structured, how they are made up of smaller meaningful parts. The smallest structure of a word is called the morphemes. Believe -> believable -> unbelievable
*Syntax*: is concerned with the ways words go together to form sentences, and how the words are related to one another. The student frowned at the teacher.
*Semantics*: concerned with the aspects of meaning that are given by words and grammar. ring in the uk means call but it doesn't in america
*Pragmatics*: handles the aspects of meaning of an utterance that come from its use in a particular context. (Hey, how's it going?). It means the cultural and interpersonal context of the communication

## Development of Linguistics Branches
*Developing Morphology:*
Uses inflectional morphemes by 2.5 years old (ing, -s)
Overgeneralization (foots/feet, holded)
*Developing Syntax:*
Developing syntactic structures (forming questions/negatives)
*Developing Semantics:*
Children use limited vocabulary during two-word stage to refer to a large number of unrelated objects (overextension of meaning)

## Intro to Phonetics: Key Concepts
- *Phoneme*: a phonological segment that can be phonetically predicted by a rule. /b/ in bit and /p/ in pit
- *Vowel:* the sounds in the production of which no articulators come very close together and the air-stream passes through the vocal tract without obstructions
- *Consonant*: the sounds in the production of which there is an obstruction of the air-stream at some point of the vocal tract
